doc.title: James Lincoln Collier interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: Jazz as an art form and the underground; Utica clubs
summary: Jazz was called an art form but felt like rebel music; Tommy Jordie's in Utica and sitting in at a black club.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: I don’t know if you would have ever had this conversation with your bandmates or your listening mates, but do you recall if you thought of this music at the time as an art form?

Oh yeah sure. I mean everyone was calling it an art form. I mean you can go back to the early 1920s there were critics who were calling it an art form. This was major critics. Critics for the New York Times used the word art in respect to jazz in the early 1920’s. So this was sort of understood it was an art form. But it was underground. The kids today of course see jazz as part of the establishment, and you know this is bad news, this is not merely your father’s music but your grandfather’s music. And so that’s a sort of an establishment thing. But we were like rock & roll guys in the fifties. We were the underground. We were the rebels. We were the outsiders. That was the way you felt about yourself and that’s the way you felt about jazz. And it was partly true. It depended where you were. In New York City no, I mean there was a lot of jazz around. But there was a good jazz club in Utica though, Tommy Jordie’s.

Yeah, I remember hearing some pretty good piano players up there if I could ever afford to go up there, which — Tommy Jordie’s. I remember hearing Joe Sullivan who was one of our heroes in — a piano player up there, a lot of piano players used to go through that place. So there was some jazz up there but basically no. There was a black club we used to go up and sit in with some of these guys. I remember the drummer had wooden leg.

I don’t know how he managed but he did. And we used to go and sit in there and I think they were bemused as well at these young white kids coming in there and banging around on our instruments the way we did.
